chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Angel Investing Really Is

lessons.title: What Is Angel Investing? Backing a Company Before It Is Proven

children.text: Arjun, a friend from engineering college, quits his job at a Bengaluru fintech to build an app that helps Nashik grape farmers sell directly to exporters. Six months in, he has 400 farmers using a rough version of the product, no revenue, and a message for you: "We are raising ₹2 crore. Can you put in ₹10 lakh?" If you say yes, you are an angel investor. This lesson explains exactly what you would be buying, how your ownership is calculated, the three ways the story can end, and why most people who write that cheque should write a much smaller one.

body.text: An angel investor buys a small piece of a company before anyone knows if it works. You are not lending money and you are not buying a stock you can sell tomorrow. You are betting that a tiny, unproven business becomes a large one, and accepting that it probably will not.

children.text: What Angel Investing Actually Is

markDefs.definition: Ownership in a company, held as shares. If the company grows in value, so does your stake. If it shuts down, the shares are usually worth nothing.
The value placed on the whole company when it raises money. At the angel stage it is negotiated between founders and investors, not derived from profits.

children.text: Angel investing means an individual putting their own money into an early-stage, unlisted startup in exchange for
equity

. The word that matters is own. A venture capital fund invests other people's money under a written mandate. An angel invests personal savings, decides alone or with a small group, and usually comes in at the earliest stage, when the company is just founders, a product in progress and a
valuation
that is closer to an educated guess than a calculation.
Three features separate an angel cheque from almost everything else in your portfolio:
You own, you are not owed.
There is no interest, no EMI and no promise of repayment. If the company fails, you get nothing back and have no claim on the founder personally.
The shares are unlisted.
You cannot sell them on NSE or BSE. Money usually comes back only when the company is acquired, lists through an IPO, or a later investor buys your shares.
The timeline is long.
Seven to ten years between cheque and exit is normal, and many startups never reach an exit at all.

children.text: How an Angel Cheque Works: Arjun's Round
Go back to Arjun's company. Call it KhetSetu. Here is what happens, step by step, if you invest.

markDefs.definition: What the company is agreed to be worth before the new money from the round comes in.

children.text: Agree a valuation.
Arjun and the incoming angels agree KhetSetu is worth ₹8 crore before any new money arrives. This is the
pre-money valuation

markDefs.definition: The pre-money valuation plus the new money raised in the round.

children.text: Raise the round.
KhetSetu raises ₹2 crore from you and a handful of other angels. The company is now worth ₹8 crore + ₹2 crore = ₹10 crore. This is the
post-money valuation
Receive shares.
KhetSetu issues new shares to you. Your ₹10 lakh buys a slice of a ₹10 crore company.
Wait.
The money pays for salaries, product development and farmer onboarding. You receive periodic updates from Arjun, not dividends.

body.caption: ₹10 crore is ₹1,000 lakh, so ₹10 lakh buys 1% of KhetSetu.

body.title: Size your stake
body.prompt: Neha invests ₹25 lakh in the same KhetSetu round at a ₹10 crore post-money valuation. What percentage of the company does she own?
body.explanation: ₹25 lakh ÷ ₹1,000 lakh = 0.025, or 2.5%. Always divide by the post-money valuation, because the new money raised in the round, including Neha's own cheque, is part of what the company is worth afterwards.

body.text: Your 1% will not stay 1%. Every time KhetSetu raises another round, it issues new shares and your percentage shrinks. This is called dilution, and Chapter 2 walks through the maths. Dilution is not bad by itself: a smaller slice of a much bigger company can be worth far more than a large slice of a small one.

children.text: The Three Ways the Story Ends

markDefs.definition: The event that turns your shares back into cash: an acquisition, an IPO, or a sale of your shares to another investor.

children.text: Assume KhetSetu raises two more rounds over the next few years, diluting your 1% to 0.8% after the first and 0.4% after the second. Here are the three broad ways your investment reaches an
exit
, or never does. The figures are simplified and ignore the special terms later investors often negotiate.

cells: KhetSetu runs out of money in year 3
A larger agritech company buys KhetSetu for ₹15 crore in year 5
KhetSetu lists on NSE and BSE at a ₹1,000 crore valuation in year 9

children.text: Look closely at the middle row. Getting 1.2x back after five years works out to under 4% a year, less than a fixed deposit, for taking far more risk. For an angel, an exit that returns your money with a little extra is a disappointment dressed up as a success. Only the rare big exit makes the risk worthwhile.

body.title: Set your expectations
body.question: For a single seed-stage startup, which ending should a new angel treat as the most likely?
options: A big exit, because the founder is talented
A modest acquisition that roughly returns the money
Losing most or all of the investment
Steady dividend income from year two
body.explanation: Most early-stage startups fail or return less than was invested. A talented founder improves the odds but does not change the base rate. Unlisted startups also almost never pay dividends, because every rupee is reinvested into growth.

children.text: Why Angels Still Do It: One Winner Pays for Everything

If most bets fail, why invest at all? Because the payoffs are lopsided. Your loss on any single startup is capped at 100% of the cheque, while a winner can return 20x, 50x or more. Picture an angel who puts ₹10 lakh each into 10 startups, ₹1 crore in total, and sees these results after eight years:

The portfolio returns ₹2.3 crore on ₹1 crore invested, or 2.3x, which works out to roughly 11% a year over eight years. Now remove the one winner: ₹30 lakh back on ₹1 crore, a 70% loss. The entire result rests on a single company, and nobody knows in advance which one it will be. This pattern is called the power law, and Chapter 3 is built around it.
Angel Investing in India: Real Examples

Some of India's best-known companies took early money long before they were household names. After retiring as chairman of Tata Sons, Ratan Tata backed startups in his personal capacity, including Ola, Paytm and Urban Company around 2015. Info Edge, the listed parent of Naukri.com, is a company rather than an individual angel, but its Zomato bet shows the same logic: a first cheque of ₹4.7 crore in August 2010, about ₹86 crore invested in total by 2013, and a stake worth thousands of crores by the time Zomato listed on NSE and BSE in July 2021.
For every Zomato, though, a large number of funded Indian startups quietly shut down. You hear about the winners because winners make the news.

children.text: What You Are Really Signing Up For

columns.label: What angels get
points: A chance at returns of 20x or more on a single company
Ownership in businesses not available on any stock exchange
A front-row view of how companies are built, and sometimes a voice as an adviser
The ability to back founders and sectors you genuinely understand

columns.label: What angels give up
points: Liquidity: money can be stuck for 7 to 10 years, or for good
Diversification: each cheque is one company, one team, one idea
Information: no quarterly results to check on screener.in, only founder updates
Protection: none of the disclosure rules SEBI applies to listed companies, and a real chance of losing everything

body.label: The first rule of angel investing
body.value: Invest only money you can afford to lose completely
body.context: Experienced angels commonly keep total startup exposure to a small slice of their investable wealth, often cited as 5 to 10%, and spread it across many companies.

children.text: The term comes from Broadway in New York, where wealthy patrons in the early twentieth century funded theatre productions that would otherwise never have opened, often knowing they would lose money. In 1978, William Wetzel, a professor at the University of New Hampshire, used the word to describe individuals who fund early-stage businesses, and it stuck. In India, organised angel investing took off with the launch of the Indian Angel Network in 2006.

body.text: Real startup rounds never promise returns. If a "startup investment" offer on WhatsApp or Telegram guarantees 3x in two years, fixed monthly payouts or a buyback at a premium, it is not angel investing. It is almost certainly a scam. Genuine angel deals come with shares, signed legal agreements and real risk.

body.title: Should Priya write the cheque?
body.scenario: Priya is a 32-year-old product manager in Pune with ₹18 lakh in savings: ₹6 lakh in an FD kept as her emergency fund and ₹12 lakh in Nifty 50 index funds. A former colleague's edtech startup is raising a seed round and asks her for ₹8 lakh. Priya likes the founder and has used the product.
body.prompt: Should Priya invest ₹8 lakh? Using what you learned in this lesson, what would you tell her?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The size is the problem, not the idea. ₹8 lakh is about 44% of her total savings, far above the small slice experienced angels put into startups.
2. To fund it, she would have to break her emergency fund or sell most of her index funds, swapping liquid, diversified money for one illiquid bet.
3. The most likely outcome for any single seed-stage startup is losing most or all of the money, however much she likes the founder.
4. Even a modest exit could take five years or more and still fail to beat her FD.
5. A more sensible path: if she wants startup exposure, she can invest a much smaller amount she can afford to lose entirely, ask for the post-money valuation so she knows her exact stake, and plan to spread future cheques across several startups. Liking the founder is a reason to look closer, not a reason to skip the maths.

body.title: The ownership formula
body.textWithBlank: To calculate your ownership in a startup round, divide your investment by the ___ valuation.
body.explanation: Your ownership = your investment ÷ post-money valuation. The post-money figure includes all the new money raised in the round, including yours.

cards.definition: An individual who invests personal money in an early-stage, unlisted startup in exchange for shares.
Ownership in a company held as shares. Worth nothing if the company fails.
What the startup is agreed to be worth before the new money from a round comes in.
Pre-money valuation plus the new money raised in the round.
The fall in your ownership percentage when the company issues new shares in later rounds.
The event that turns your shares back into cash: an acquisition, an IPO or a sale to another investor.

points: An angel investor puts personal money into an early-stage, unlisted startup in exchange for shares, not a promise of repayment.
Ownership = investment ÷ post-money valuation. ₹10 lakh at a ₹10 crore post-money valuation buys 1%.
Your percentage shrinks with every later round, but a smaller slice of a much bigger company can still be worth far more.
The most likely outcome for any single startup is losing most or all of the money, and even a modest exit can underperform an FD.
Returns come from rare big winners, which is why angels spread small cheques across many companies.
Invest only money you can afford to lose completely, and treat any startup deal promising fixed returns as a red flag.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice or a recommendation to invest in any company named here. Startup investments are high risk and illiquid, and can result in total loss of capital. KhetSetu, Arjun, Neha and Priya are illustrative. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
